Tech Enthusiasts are welcomed.

🚀 Project Concept: FLARE-X

FLARE-X — Fire & Flame Risk Analytics Explorer

Tagline:

“From NASA's fire experiments to an AI copilot for safer spacecraft.”

The core product has three layers:

                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │      NASA DATA HUB       │
                  │ Saffire • BASS • FLEX    │
                  │ Experiments • Papers     │
                  └────────────┬─────────────┘
                               ↓
                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │   AI FIRE INTELLIGENCE   │
                  │                          │
                  │ RAG + ML + CV + Ranking  │
                  │ Anomaly Detection        │
                  │ Risk Prediction          │
                  └────────────┬─────────────┘
                               ↓
             ┌─────────────────┼──────────────────┐
             ↓                 ↓                  ↓
      🔥 FIRE RISK       🔬 EXPERIMENT       🤖 AI COPILOT
      SCORE              EXPLORER             "Ask NASA Data"
             ↓                 ↓                  ↓
      LOW/MED/HIGH       Compare tests       Evidence-backed
      risk factors       & materials         answers

This is much stronger than:

“Here is a dashboard showing NASA experiments.”

Instead:

“We transformed decades of fragmented combustion experiments into an explainable fire-risk intelligence layer.”

1. The most important insight

NASA already has an enormous body of research.

For example:

Saffire investigated large-scale flame growth and material flammability in spacecraft-like environments.

BASS/BASS-II studied ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction.

FLEX studied liquid-droplet combustion and extinction limits.

NASA's data repository contains raw experimental material and engineering documentation.

NASA says Saffire generated data on things such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure, flame growth and imagery. NASA Science

BASS-II investigated forced flow velocity, oxygen concentration, fuel geometry, flame appearance, growth, spread and extinction. NASA Science

FLEX focused on flammability limits and suppressant effectiveness under microgravity. NASA Science

So your project can unify these.

2. The killer feature: Fire Risk Score

This should be the centerpiece.

Why?

Then:

AI Recommendation

Important: Don't claim this is an actual NASA operational safety rating. Label it:

Prototype AI-derived comparative risk score — not an operational NASA safety certification.

That scientific honesty will actually make your project stronger.

3. Make it explainable

Don't just say:

Risk = 78

Show why.

And underneath:

Now you're building scientific interpretability, not an arbitrary ML model.

NASA's PSI repository provides exactly the kind of experimental metadata and raw data you can build around. For example, the Saffire-I record lists cameras, thermocouples, radiometers, pressure/O₂/CO₂ sensors and airflow measurements. NASA Science

This directly addresses the challenge's problem of making decades of results easier to compare.

6. The AI Copilot

This is where your AI/ML background becomes valuable.

Call it:

FLARE Copilot

User asks:

Why does fire behave differently in microgravity?

Answer:

In microgravity, buoyancy-driven convection is greatly reduced, changing how heat and combustion products move around the flame. NASA observations show that low-gravity flames can become rounded or spherical compared with the familiar upward flame shape on Earth. NASA

Then:

Evidence

Saffire-I
BASS-II
NASA Combustion Science

And links to the source experiment.

8. ML component

You should have an actual ML model.

Otherwise judges may ask:

    airflow,
    pressure,
    material,
    geometry,
    gravity
)

Option C — safest choice

Predict:

Extinction probability

I recommend Option C + a risk score.

Then SHAP:

Material                +17
Airflow                 +12
Pressure                 +7

This gives you real ML + explainability.

24. What NOT to do

This is important.

❌ Don't build:

“NASA experiment search website”

Too basic.

❌ Don't build:

“ChatGPT connected to NASA PDFs”

Too generic.

❌ Don't build:

“Random AI fire prediction”

Scientifically weak.

❌ Don't build:

Huge 3D spacecraft visualization

Time sink.

❌ Don't claim:

“Our AI predicts actual spacecraft fires.”

Instead:

“Our prototype estimates comparative fire-risk patterns from historical NASA experimental data.”

Much more defensible.

25. Research questions for your team

Before coding, investigate these.

Research Question 1

How does microgravity change flame geometry?

NASA notes that without normal buoyancy, low-momentum flames can become rounded/spherical. NASA

Research Question 2

How do oxygen concentration and airflow affect flame spread?

BASS-II explicitly varies oxygen concentration and forced flow. NASA Science

Research Question 3

What determines flame extinction?

FLEX is particularly useful here because it investigates limiting oxygen conditions and suppressant effectiveness. NASA Science

Research Question 4

How does scale affect fire behavior?

This is very interesting.

Saffire demonstrated that large-scale microgravity flames can behave differently from smaller experimental setups. NASA Technical Reports Server

That could become one of your major insights.

Research Question 5

Can historical experiments predict behavior in new conditions?

This becomes your ML research question.

26. Your research hypothesis

Put this in the project.

Hypothesis:
A unified model combining environmental conditions, material properties, experimental geometry and flame behavior can identify comparable historical microgravity combustion experiments and estimate relative fire-risk and extinction behavior for previously unseen operating conditions.

That's a legitimate ML research question.

30. Team description

You can use this:

We are AI and technology enthusiasts building an intelligent fire-safety system for the next generation of human space exploration.

For the “Flame in Freefall” challenge, our goal is to transform NASA’s decades of microgravity combustion research into an interactive AI-powered platform that makes complex fire behavior easier to explore, compare, and understand.

Our project combines NASA experimental data, machine learning, computer vision, retrieval-augmented AI, data visualization, and explainable risk analysis to help answer questions such as: How does a flame behave under different microgravity conditions? Which historical NASA experiments are most comparable? What factors increase or decrease fire risk? And what can these findings teach us about future Moon, Mars, and deep-space habitats?

We welcome teammates interested in AI/ML, data science, software engineering, frontend development, scientific research, UX/design, visualization, space science, and storytelling.

If you are excited about using technology to solve real problems in human space exploration, join us and help turn NASA’s combustion data into actionable fire-safety intelligence.

For Languages Spoken, select:

English + Hindi if those are appropriate for your team.

For Accepting Team Members, I'd keep it checked until your core team is complete.

43. The three things judges should remember

After your presentation, a judge should remember only these:

1. We unified NASA's combustion knowledge.

Not just one dataset.

2. We turned it into explainable AI.

Not just a chatbot.

3. We made it useful for future spacecraft.

Not just historical analysis.

44. What makes this potentially competitive

NASA itself notes that Saffire data can help understand flame growth, combustion products and vehicle effects, while research such as BASS contributes to computational models for fire detection and suppression. NASA

So your story has a very natural progression:

PAST
NASA experiments
       ↓
PRESENT
AI organizes + understands them
       ↓
FUTURE
Moon / Mars spacecraft fire safety

That is the story I would sell.

45. One important strategic decision

Do NOT call the system “NASA Fire Prediction AI.”

Call it:

FLARE-X — AI-Powered Microgravity Fire Safety Intelligence

And describe the model as:

summary:
FlameLens AI is an interactive, SI-powered dashboard designed to make NASA's microgravity fire and combustion research easier to understand and use.
Fire behaves very differently in space because microgravity changes airflow and flame behavior. NASA has collected decades of valuable experimental data, but this information can be difficult to search, compare, and interpret.
Our solution uses AI and data visualization to organize microgravity combustion data and turn it into clear fire-safety insights. Users can search for experiments, compare different conditions such as fuel and oxygen levels, visualize results, and receive AI-generated summaries.
A key feature is the Fire Safety Insight Ranking, which highlights the most important findings for astronaut safety. The platform also includes an “Ask the Fire Data” AI assistant, allowing users to ask questions in simple language and understand complex research quickly.

1. The most important insight

NASA already has an enormous body of research.

For example:

  • BASS/BASS-II studied ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction.
  • FLEX studied liquid-droplet combustion and extinction limits.
  • NASA's data repository contains raw experimental material and engineering documentation.

NASA says Saffire generated data on things such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, heat, pressure, flame growth and imagery. NASA Science

BASS-II investigated forced flow velocity, oxygen concentration, fuel geometry, flame appearance, growth, spread and extinction. NASA Science

FLEX focused on flammability limits and suppressant effectiveness under microgravity. NASA Science

25. Research questions for your team

Before coding, investigate these.

Research Question 1

How does microgravity change flame geometry?

NASA notes that without normal buoyancy, low-momentum flames can become rounded/spherical. NASA

Research Question 2

How do oxygen concentration and airflow affect flame spread?

BASS-II explicitly varies oxygen concentration and forced flow. NASA Science

Research Question 3

What determines flame extinction?

FLEX is particularly useful here because it investigates limiting oxygen conditions and suppressant effectiveness. NASA Science

Research Question 4

How does scale affect fire behavior?

This is very interesting.

Saffire demonstrated that large-scale microgravity flames can behave differently from smaller experimental setups. NASA Technical Reports Server

That could become one of your major insights.

Research Question 5

Can historical experiments predict behavior in new conditions?

This becomes your ML research question.
